vignette:
Kwame was just beginning to carve out a promising career as a journalist when the traumatic incident unfolded. At 25, he was passionate about uncovering stories that mattered, and he often focused on social justice issues within marginalized communities. However, everything changed one fateful evening when he was covering a protest against police brutality. As tensions escalated, he found himself caught in the chaos. The flash of lights, the shouts, and the heavy boots of officers rushing past him left an indelible mark on his psyche. When he heard the sharp crack of a baton striking against a nearby protestor, his heart raced, and his world seemed to close in around him. It was not just the violence he witnessed but the deep sense of helplessness that washed over him. 

Ever since that day, Kwame's reality had shifted drastically. He now lived in a constant state of hyper-awareness, and his sense of safety felt irrevocably shattered. Everyday sounds that once blended into the background began to take on an ominous quality. The sound of footsteps behind him sent a jolt of panic through his body; he would often find himself halting mid-stride, glancing over his shoulder to check if someone was following him. He had come to believe that he could no longer trust his surroundings, and unfamiliar places became a minefield of potential threats. His friends noticed his increasing reluctance to join them for outings; he started to avoid events that might pull him into crowded spaces or, worse, remind him of that fateful night.

As time passed, Kwame realized he was avoiding more than just physical locations. He meticulously curated his wardrobe, opting for oversized, concealing clothing that made him feel less noticeable. The very act of dressing became laden with anxiety; he had to ensure he didn't draw attention to himself, fearing that being seen would make him vulnerable again. Even music, a passion he once cherished, turned into a source of distress. Certain songs, once beloved, now replayed in his mind with haunting memories attached, making him avoid them at all costs. Anything that reminded him of his lost sense of safety or the friends he had lost in the chaos became a trigger, and he steered clear of those reminders with calculated precision.

Kwame's internal world was tumultuous. He found it increasingly difficult to concentrate, and the demands of his job felt overwhelming. Writing, which had been his lifeline, transformed into a struggle as he grappled with a foggy mind. He often felt that his memories of the traumatic event were more vivid than anything else in his life, overwhelming him whenever he tried to articulate his experience. The words would escape him, and he would lose the thread of his thoughts, feeling lost and incapable of expressing what had transpired. This difficulty only compounded the feelings of inadequacy that had taken root in him; he believed he was no longer capable of functioning as the person he once was. 

What frightened Kwame most was the sense of having lost a part of himself forever. He used to be a happy person, filled with dreams and ambitions, but now he felt like he was merely existing in a shadow of his former life. The trauma had wrapped its tendrils around every aspect of his being, and he felt utterly defeated. He began to view his life as destroyed by the events surrounding the protest, and the thought of reclaiming his former self seemed impossible.

It wasn't until he reached a breaking point—after a particularly intense episode of auditory recall where he could hear the chaotic shouts and the sound of boots thundering toward him—that Kwame sought help. He confided in his partner, who had grown increasingly concerned about his emotional withdrawal and the toll it was taking on their relationship. With a mix of hope and trepidation, Kwame made the decision to talk to a therapist, fearing that he might never be able to reclaim the joy he once felt, but also desperate for a path forward. It was a small step, but one that felt monumental in the face of his overwhelming grief and anxiety.
